core: WHERE filters rows: it keeps only the rows that meet a stated condition
Basic query shape: SELECT columns FROM table WHERE condition
Comparison operators =, <>, >, < (equal, not equal, greater than, less than)
Text values quoted, numeric values unquoted
Combining conditions with AND and OR
WHERE applies before grouping and sorting conceptually
supporting: Each row is checked against the condition one at a time; false or null results are discarded
SQL also has >= and <=; some systems accept != for not equal
WHERE appears in UPDATE and DELETE statements too (sibling topics own those)
WHERE is where most query mistakes happen; precision in conditions pays
outOfScope: SELECT clause details and column selection rules (sibling topic: select)
ORDER BY sorting behavior (sibling topic: order-by)
GROUP BY grouping and HAVING (sibling topic: group-by)
UPDATE and DELETE statement mechanics (sibling topics: update, delete)
LIKE, BETWEEN, IN and other advanced operators
NULL-handling subtleties beyond the keep-if-true rule

claims.claim: The WHERE clause filters rows: it keeps only the rows that fulfill a stated condition and discards the rest.
The basic shape of a filtering query is SELECT column1, column2 FROM table_name WHERE condition.
Comparison operators in WHERE include = (equal), <> (not equal; some systems also accept !=), > (greater than), and < (less than), plus >= and <=.
Text values in conditions are written inside single quotes, while numeric values are written without quotes.
AND combines conditions so a row must satisfy all of them; OR combines conditions so a row is kept if it satisfies at least one.

After the FROM clause is processed, each row of the derived table is checked against the WHERE search condition; the row is kept only when the condition is true and discarded when it is false or null.

Conceptually, WHERE narrows the row set before grouping and sorting are applied; the documentation describes FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, and HAVING as a pipeline of successive transformations on the table.
WHERE is also used in UPDATE and DELETE statements, not only in SELECT.

positions: Standard SQL writes not equal as <>
Some database systems also accept != (and a few legacy systems use != or ^=)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson teaches <> as the standard form and notes that != appears in some systems; examples use <>.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether WHERE changes the underlying table
positions: Students sometimes expect a filtered query to remove rows from the table
WHERE only affects the rows returned by that query; the table itself is unchanged
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson states explicitly that WHERE filters the result without altering the stored rows; supported by PostgreSQL's description of the derived virtual table.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's claim that WHERE is a foundational concept best taught as context and application carried no factual content and was replaced with the source-verified filter definition.
The draft's vocabulary definitions (e.g., 'context: the situation or conditions that shape how an idea is understood') were generic filler with no connection to SQL and were replaced.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the machine-generated boilerplate lesson (which never mentioned filtering or conditions) with a source-verified lesson about WHERE as a row filter.
All example queries are original and were executed against an in-memory SQLite table to confirm correct results before publishing.
